hops.afterHeading: What the rule explains: specificity, cooperativity, associativity
hops.title: Spike order can affect whether some synapses strengthen or weaken
hops.text: Donald Hebb never wrote "cells that fire together, wire together." Carla Shatz used it in 1992 to explain activity-dependent wiring in the developing visual system. Unlike that line, Hebb's 1949 rule was directional: one cell repeatedly helps fire another. Later, order turned out to matter on a millisecond scale. In cultured rat hippocampal neurons, Guo-Qiang Bi and Mu-ming Poo repeatedly paired an input with a spike in the receiving cell. At synapses that started weak, a spike within 20 milliseconds after the input produced LTP. A spike within 20 milliseconds before the input produced LTD instead. Both needed NMDA receptors, and neither appeared when the receiving cell was inhibitory.

sources.citation: Markram, Gerstner & Sjöström, Front. Synaptic Neurosci. 3:4 (2011)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two relay runners passing a golden baton in the right order on a sunny track, while behind them another pair stumbles because the second runner left too early.
image.caption: At these weak synapses, repeated input-before-spike pairings within 20 milliseconds strengthened the connection; reversing the order weakened it.

hops.title: Lambert-Eaton syndrome: a weak signal that grows with a hard squeeze
hops.text: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome turns residual Ca2+ into a clinical sign. In about 90 percent of patients, antibodies target the P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in motor nerve terminals, so each impulse lets in too little Ca2+ and releases too little acetylcholine. Muscles are weak and tendon reflexes are reduced or absent. In a standard test, the patient contracts a muscle as hard as they can for 10 to 30 seconds. The rapid firing lets Ca2+ build up in the terminals, and immediately afterward the evoked electrical response of the muscle can more than double. Reflexes can be amplified afterward too, which is why clinicians test strength and reflexes after rest.

sources.citation: Ivanovski & Miralles, Degener. Neurol. Neuromuscul. Dis. 9:27–37 (2019)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand squeezing a yellow foam grip ball on a wooden table beside a reflex hammer and a small potted plant.
image.caption: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, residual Ca2+ can more than double the muscle's evoked electrical response just after a brief contraction.

hops.afterHeading: From synapse to memory: what the evidence licenses
hops.title: The "Doogie" mice that learned better and reacted more to pain
hops.text: In 1999 Ya-Ping Tang, Joe Tsien and colleagues made mice that overexpressed NR2B (GluN2B) in the adult forebrain, prolonging NMDA receptor currents. CA1 LTP was stronger, and the mice beat their littermates at recognizing familiar objects and finding a hidden platform in a water maze. They came to be called "Doogie" mice. In 2001 Feng Wei, Min Zhuo and colleagues tested mice with the same forebrain NR2B overexpression for pain. Acute pain tests matched controls, but responses to lingering inflammatory pain were enhanced, with stronger NMDA responses in two forebrain pain areas. Tang and Tsien's reply was titled "Do 'smart' mice feel more pain, or are they just better learners?"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A brown lab mouse resting on a hidden platform just beneath the surface of a round pool of milky water.
image.caption: Mice with extra NR2B did better on memory tasks and also responded more to lingering inflammatory pain.

audio.title: Smarter mice, spaced bursts and synapses that shrink in sleep
audio.transcript:
Here are three experiments about turning synapses up and down, and each one came with a catch.

The first asks what happens when mice make extra N R two B, a subunit that can make N M D A receptor currents last longer. In nineteen ninety-nine, Ya-Ping Tang, Joe Tsien and colleagues at Princeton made mice that overexpressed N R two B in the adult forebrain. The receptors' currents lasted longer. Their C A one synapses showed stronger L T P, and the mice did better at recognizing familiar objects and at finding a hidden platform in a water maze. They came to be called Doogie mice. Two years later, Feng Wei, Min Zhuo and colleagues tested mice with the same forebrain N R two B overexpression for pain. On acute pain tests, they were indistinguishable from ordinary mice. Their responses to persistent inflammation were enhanced, and two forebrain pain regions, the anterior cingulate and the insular cortex, had stronger N M D A responses. Tang and Tsien answered with a comment whose title asked whether smart mice feel more pain, or are just better learners. Tang's group had argued that N R two B gates the age-dependent threshold for plasticity, and a gate like that does not act on memory circuits alone.

The second experiment is about timing. In two thousand twelve, Enikö Kramár, Gary Lynch and colleagues gave adult rat hippocampal slices a train of theta burst stimulation, enough that L T P seemed saturated. A second train given ten or thirty minutes later briefly boosted the response, without adding lasting potentiation. Given sixty or ninety minutes later, the same train pushed L T P markedly higher. Two further experiments suggested why. In adult mouse slices, stimulating single spines caused about forty percent of the targeted small spines to enlarge. A separate stain for potentiated spines indicated that the delayed train recruited synapses the first one had missed. This is a result in brain slices, not a study schedule. Still, it gives a cellular version of what psychologists call the spacing effect: the same amount of stimulation does more when it is spread out.

The third asks what happens after a day of turning synapses up. In two thousand seventeen, Luisa de Vivo, Chiara Cirelli, Giulio Tononi and colleagues used three-D electron microscopy to measure six thousand nine hundred twenty synapses in mouse motor and sensory cortex. After sleep, the contact area between axon and spine was about eighteen percent smaller on average than after wake. The difference was concentrated in the smaller four fifths of synapses. The largest fifth showed no clear change on average. In the same issue of Science, Graham Diering and colleagues reported that synapses in sleeping mice weaken through removal and dephosphorylation of A M P A receptors, the receptors this lesson adds in L T P and removes in L T D. The authors propose that sleep renormalizes synaptic strength after a day of learning. If they are right, turning synapses down is not simple decay. The sleep and wake comparisons point to an active process linked to sleep.
